newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl ready for talks on German jobs crisis.
newsitem.headline: Kohl ready for talks on German jobs crisis.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Thursday said Germany's economic recovery was soundly based but declared himself ready to hold new talks with company and trade union bosses to try to beat a jobs crisis.

Speaking after the latest data showed that December unemployment hit a postwar record of 4.156 million, seasonally adjusted, Kohl said his goal of halving dole queues by the year 2000 would be difficult -- but not impossible -- to achieve.
"Fighting unemployment remains the most important domestic policy challenge," Kohl told a news conference. "Current levels of over 4.1 million jobless are completely unacceptable."

Kohl said he was ready to chair a new round of policy talks with company executives and union leaders. Similar talks last year on building an "alliance for jobs" collapsed over labour resistance to his government's austerity policies.
But, although he was ready "day and night" to reopen talks, he said they could only resume without preconditions.
The 14-year-old Kohl government's belt-tightening is aimed at ensuring Bonn meets the Maastricht treaty's tough borrowing limits to qualify for European economic and monetary union (EMU).
Kohl, who wants the euro single currency to be launched on time in 1999, said he opposed a German referendum on EMU.
He cited a clause in the postwar constitution barring plebiscites -- designed to eliminate the instability of the 1920s Weimar Republic.
But he said he was confident of winning over a sceptical German public to the cause of monetary union in the end.
"I am confident that when...people have all the information, we will get a clear majority of the population for the euro," the Chancellor said.
Attacking Kohl on the economy, the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) said his government offered "no ideas and vague promises" on overcoming Germany's worst jobs crisis since the 1930s.
"Mass unemployment threatens social stability in Germany," SPD economics spokesman Ernst Schwanhold said.
December jobless figures without seasonal adjustment surged to 4.148 million, or 10.8 percent of the workforce, and could hit 4.5 million this winter, Federal Labour Office head Bernhard Jagoda said.

Kohl said immigration from eastern Europe after the fall of the Berlin Wall had been one cause of rising unemployment. But he said he could not understand why firms were shedding staff while the remaining workers were racking up record overtime.
Cutting back overtime could create hundreds of thousands of new jobs, he said.
Despite record unemployment, Kohl said: "Chances for recovery rest on a solid basis...I see no grounds for resignation. Creating jobs is possible."
Underpinning prospects for economic recovery were low interest rates, price stability, a positive global economic outlook, a weaker mark and moderate wage settlements, he said.
Kohl also dismissed as unfounded a downbeat forecast by the influential DIW research institute -- one of a panel of six whose forecasts underpin budget policy.

The Berlin-based DIW -- closely linked to the SPD and trade unions -- predicted this week that gross domestic product (GDP) would rise by just two percent in 1997. But Kohl said he still backed the six institutes' autumn forecast of 2.5 percent growth.

Preliminary data showed on Thursday that the economy grew a sluggish 1.4 percent in 1996, while the budget deficit jumped to 3.9 percent of GDP -- above the Maastricht ceiling of three percent, the Federal Statistics Office said.
Kohl's coalition is in the home stretch of arduous talks on drafting a common strategy to streamline Germany's tax system and help keep down state borrowing in the long term.

He said a coalition working group would complete its work this month on a strategy to cut income taxes and scrap a range of tax breaks from 1999. But consultations over thrashing out final legislation would continue all year, he added.
